title: Darshan: the deity looks back
hook: the temple curtain opens, and a crowd leans in to see the deity and be seen
carry: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen
tomorrow: How does the Gita say to sit?

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka as dharana you can see: dharana: the mind held on one beloved form.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `DHARANA: THE MIND HELD ON ONE BELOVED FORM.`

segments.voice: Evening at a temple. A small crowd stands packed in front of a closed curtain, shoes left at the door, hands holding flowers and little plates of sweets. Bells. Then the curtain is drawn aside, the lamp is lifted, and there is the image of the deity, dressed and garlanded, eyes wide. Nobody in the crowd looks away. Some fold their hands. A grandfather lifts a small boy higher so he can see. This is darshan. When the thing you gaze at is not a mark on a wall, what changes?
screen: `THE CURTAIN IS DRAWN ASIDE.` → `A CROWD LEANS IN TO SEE.` → `WHAT IF THE MARK IS SACRED?`

segments.voice: Darshan means seeing, or a sight. In temple worship it names the moment of beholding the deity in the image, the murti. People go to the temple for darshan the way they'd go to visit family. And the teaching underneath is this: for the devotee, God is truly present in the murti, so darshan isn't only looking. As many devotees describe it, the deity is also looking back. The worshipper sees, and is seen. That's why a murti's eyes are so wide, and why in many temples the eyes of a new image are the last part to be opened, in a rite of their own. The Bhagavad Gita has a scene about the limits of that seeing. In chapter eleven, Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his supreme form. And Krishna answers, in paraphrase: you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my power. Then the vision comes, vast and blazing, more than Arjuna can hold, and he begs to see the familiar, gentle form again. Many teachers read the murti in that light: God, who is more than any eye can hold, takes a form a person can look at, and lets himself be seen. Some who practice trataka choose a sacred image as their point. The method stays the same: a steady gaze, a gentle return. But the gaze is now attention offered to someone. Teachers differ: some keep trataka to a flame, others welcome a sacred image.
screen: `DARSHAN: SEEING, AND BEING SEEN.` · `GOD PRESENT IN THE MURTI.` · `ARJUNA IS GIVEN A DIVINE EYE.` · `A FORM YOU CAN LOOK AT.` · then, large: `THE IMAGE LOOKS BACK.`

segments.voice: If you keep a sacred image, a deity, a symbol, a photo of a teacher, set it at eye level; if not, a flame or a simple mark is just as good. Rest the eyes on it softly, blinking when you need to, and if it's an image that matters to you, let the gaze feel like a greeting rather than a stare. When the eyes tire, close them and hold what stays, then look again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, its neighbor darshan, where the gaze rests on a sacred image, and the worshipper sees and is seen.
Your line: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen. The image, this time, looks back. Rest well.
